content: An F-test is a type of statistical test where the test statistic follows an F-distribution under the assumption that the null hypothesis is true. The term F-test was named by George W. Snedecor in honor of Sir Ronald A. Fisher, who originally developed the statistic as the variance ratio in the 1920s. One common application of the F-test is to evaluate the hypothesis that the means of multiple normally distributed populations, all of which share the same standard deviation, are equal. This is the most widely recognized use of the F-test and represents the simplest scenario in the analysis of variance (ANOVA). Another application of the F-test is to test the hypothesis that the standard deviations of two normally distributed populations are equal, implying that the populations are of comparable origin. However, it is important to note that when testing for equality of variances (or standard deviations), the F-test is highly sensitive to deviations from normality. Even minor departures from a normal distribution can render the test unreliable, making it unsuitable for use in such cases. In many situations, the F-test statistic can be calculated through a straightforward process. This involves comparing two regression models: one that imposes constraints on one or more regression coefficients based on the null hypothesis, and another that does not. The test statistic is derived from a modified ratio of the residual sum of squares (RSS) of the two models. To illustrate, consider two models, Model 1 and Model 2, where Model 1 is nested within Model 2. Model 1 has ( p_1 ) parameters, while Model 2 has ( p_2 ) parameters, with ( p_2 > p_1 ). The number of parameters includes any constant terms in the model. For example, a simple linear model ( y = mx + b ) would have ( p = 2 ) parameters under this convention. If there are ( n ) data points available to estimate the parameters of both models, the F statistic is calculated as follows: [ F = frac{left( text{RSS}_1 text{RSS}_2 right) / (p_2 p_1)}{text{RSS}_2 / (n p_2)} ] Here, ( text{RSS}_i ) represents the residual sum of squares for Model ( i ). If the regression model has been calculated with weights, ( text{RSS}_i ) should be replaced with ( chi^2 ), the weighted sum of squared residuals. The F statistic follows an F-distribution with degrees of freedom ( (p_2 p_1, n p_2) ). The probability that the reduction in ( chi^2 ) associated with adding ( p_2 p_1 ) parameters is due solely to chance is determined by the probability associated with the F-distribution at that point. For example, a significance level of 0.05 is commonly used. Critical values for the F-test can be found in statistical tables or are typically included in most statistical software and textbooks.
